samples.text:
Good behaviour and respect for other people are very important qualities for children. Some people think that parents, not teachers, should be mainly responsible for teaching these things. I agree with this statement.

Firstly, children spend most of their time with their family, especially in the first years of life. Before they start school, they already learn how to speak, how to eat and how to behave with other people from their parents. If parents teach them to say "please" and "thank you" and to share with others, these habits will stay with them for all their life. Also, children usually copy what their parents do. If a father is polite with his neighbours, his son will probably learn to be polite too.

Secondly, teachers have many students in one class, sometimes more than thirty. They don't have enough time to pay attention for the behaviour of every child. Their main job is to teach subjects like maths, science and languages. If the teacher must spend a lot of time to correct bad behaviour, the other students cannot learn well.

However, teachers also have some role. At school, children learn how to work in groups, how to follow rules and how to respect people from different backgrounds. Teachers can support what the parents teach at home. But if the parents don't teach good manners, it is very difficult for teachers to change a child's behaviour.

In conclusion, I believe that parents should be mainly responsible for teaching children good behaviour and respect because children spend more time with them and learn by copying them. Teachers can help, but the main responsibility belong to the family.

samples.text:
It is often debated whether parents or teachers should take the main responsibility for teaching children to behave well and respect others. Some people believe this is primarily the role of parents. I partly agree with this view, as I think parents should lay the foundations, but schools have a vital and distinctive contribution to make.

Parents clearly have the greatest influence during a child's early years. Long before children start school, they learn how to treat others by observing the adults around them, and values such as honesty, kindness and patience are absorbed through daily routines at home. A child whose parents speak respectfully to each other and to strangers is far more likely to adopt the same attitude. Moreover, parents can give individual attention and correct behaviour consistently, which is difficult for a teacher responsible for a whole class.

However, schools provide experiences that the family cannot. In the classroom, children must cooperate with peers from different backgrounds, follow shared rules and resolve conflicts without their parents' help. These situations teach respect in a wider social context and prepare children for adult life in a diverse community. Teachers can also reinforce good behaviour through clear expectations and by being positive role models, which is particularly important for children whose home environment are less supportive.

For these reasons, I believe the responsibility should be shared. Parents are best placed to instil basic values, while teachers help children to apply them in a broader setting. When the two work together and send consistent messages, children are much more likely to develop good behaviour that lasts.

In conclusion, although parents should play the leading role in teaching manners and respect, I do not think teachers' contribution should be seen as secondary. Effective moral education depends on cooperation between home and school.

samples.text:
The question of who should teach children good behaviour and respect for others is often framed as a choice between home and school. I agree that parents should bear the primary responsibility, since the values children absorb in their earliest years are formed largely within the family. However, I would argue that teachers play an indispensable supporting role rather than a marginal one.

The strongest argument for parental responsibility lies in the timing and nature of early learning. Children's attitudes towards others begin to take shape long before they enter a classroom, and they are shaped less by explicit instruction than by imitation. A toddler who sees a parent listen patiently, apologise when wrong and treat service workers courteously internalises these patterns almost unconsciously. Parents also have a depth of knowledge about their own child and the continuity of contact over many years that no teacher, responsible for thirty pupils for a single year, can match.

There is also a question of accountability. If parents come to assume that manners and respect will be taught at school, they may neglect this aspect of upbringing, leaving teachers to address behavioural problems that divert time from learning. Recognising that the family is the first line of moral education places responsibility where it can be exercised most effectively.

That said, schools offer something that homes cannot: a structured community of peers. Learning to share resources, wait one's turn, work with classmates one did not choose and respect people from different cultures are lessons best learnt in a group setting. Teachers who model fairness and enforce consistent rules can reinforce good habits and, crucially, compensate for children who receive little guidance at home.

In conclusion, parents should be principally responsible for teaching good behaviour and respect, but this responsibility is most effectively fulfilled when schools reinforce and extend the values children first learn within the family.
